tt.title: One earthquake, seven stations, two maps
tt.mini: The 2004 Sumatra earthquake seen by seven real seismic stations. On the globe, every arrival sits on one straight line. The flat map puts Palmer Station, Antarctica, twice as far away: 59 minutes late.
tt.text: Arrival time against distance for the 2004 Sumatra–Andaman earthquake (M9.1) at seven stations of the Global Seismographic Network. Each station is plotted twice at the same arrival time: at its great-circle distance (teal) and at its distance on the usual flat-earth map, the north-polar azimuthal equidistant projection (orange). The globe puts every point on one line through the origin, at the wave's speed of 3.8 km/s [1]. The flat map is right near the North Pole and wrong everywhere else: it puts Palmer Station, Antarctica, at 26,470 km instead of 12,995 km, which is 59 minutes of travel. The arrival times here are computed on the sphere, to show the size of the disagreement; the same test on real recorded times gives the same answer.
tt.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: real recorded arrivals that line up with the flat-map distances rather than the great-circle ones.
arc.title: An earthquake measures a distance
arc.mini: An epicentre and a station on one sphere: the wave runs along the arc R × Δ, so its arrival time is RΔ/v. Every seismogram is a distance measurement between two points on Earth.
arc.text: A surface wave leaves the epicentre and runs along the ground to a station. On a sphere of radius R, that path is an arc of length RΔ, where Δ is the angle between the two points at the centre. At a wave speed v, the arrival time is RΔ/v. So every recorded arrival is a measurement of the distance between two known points. A few thousand stations record every large earthquake, so each one measures thousands of distances between every pair of continents, and those distances can be tested against any map. The sphere in the drawing is shown small.
arc.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: arrival times that match straight-line distances on a flat map better than arcs on a sphere.
wave.title: A real earthquake, on the globe and on the flat map
wave.mini: Each dot is a real seismic station and lights up at its real recorded arrival time. On the globe the dots follow the wavefront. On the flat map they leave the flat model's circle behind.
wave.text: A real earthquake and the real stations that recorded it, from the International Seismological Centre's bulletin [1]. Each dot lights up at that station's own recorded arrival time. On the globe, the wavefront is a circle that grows at 3.5 km/s from the epicentre and closes on the opposite point, and the dots light up as it reaches them. On the usual flat-earth map (the north-polar azimuthal equidistant projection): teal is the same real front drawn on the map, orange is the circle the map itself predicts at the same speed. The dots follow the teal line, not the orange one. Time is accelerated ×900.
wave.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: stations lighting up as the orange circle reaches them, not the teal front.
wave-globe.title: A real earthquake crossing the globe
wave-globe.mini: Each dot is a real seismic station and lights up at its real recorded arrival time. The wavefront is a circle that grows from the epicentre, and the dots follow it around the world.
wave-globe.text: A real earthquake and the real stations that recorded it, from the International Seismological Centre's bulletin [1]. Each dot lights up at that station's own recorded arrival time. The wavefront is computed: a circle on the sphere that grows from the epicentre at 3.5 km/s, the speed of an 18–22 s surface wave, and closes on the opposite point of the Earth. The dots light up as the circle reaches them, on every continent, with one speed and one radius, 6371 km. Time is accelerated ×900.
wave-globe.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: stations lighting up out of step with a front that grows at one speed on the sphere.
wave-map.title: A real earthquake on the flat-earth map
wave-map.mini: The usual flat-earth map, real seismic stations lighting up at their recorded arrival times. The flat map's own wavefront (orange) falls behind them. The globe's front (teal) keeps up.
wave-map.text: The background is the north-polar azimuthal equidistant projection, the standard flat-earth map, on which distance from the North Pole is correct and nothing else is. Each dot is a real station that recorded a real earthquake, and lights up at its own recorded arrival time, from the International Seismological Centre's bulletin [1]. Orange is the circle the map predicts for a wave at 3.5 km/s. Teal is the front computed on the sphere, at the same speed, and drawn onto the same map. The dots follow the teal front, not the orange circle. Time is accelerated ×900.
wave-map.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: stations lighting up as the orange circle reaches them, not the teal front.
core.title: The ring of silence
core.mini: Between about 103° and 143° from every earthquake, direct P waves do not arrive: a liquid core bends them away. A ring at the same angular distance around every epicentre is what a sphere with a core produces.
core.text: A cross-section of the Earth with P-wave paths leaving one epicentre. Rays that stay in the mantle curve back up and reach the surface out to about 103°. Rays that enter the core are bent sharply downward and come out only past about 143°. In between, no direct P wave arrives. S waves cannot cross a liquid at all, so their shadow runs from 103° to the opposite point. Oldham read the molten interior off the missing S waves in 1906 [1], Gutenberg placed the core boundary near 2,900 km depth in 1913 [2], and Lehmann found the solid inner core in 1936 from faint arrivals inside the shadow [3]. The layers are drawn to scale (core boundary at 3,480 km radius, inner core at 1,221 km [4]); the ray paths are schematic.
core.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: a shadow that is not a ring at a fixed angular distance, the same around every epicentre and in every direction.
laps.title: The wave that goes round the world
laps.mini: A large earthquake's surface wave reaches a station the short way (R1), the long way (R2), then the short way again after a full lap (R3). The gap from R1 to R3 is one trip around the planet.
laps.text: A surface wave leaves the epicentre in every direction. One station records it arriving the short way round (R1), then the long way round (R2), then the short way again after one complete extra lap (R3), and for the greatest earthquakes R4 and more. The magnitude-6.9 Loma Prieta earthquake of 1989 produced clean R1, R2 and R3 across the world's stations [1]. The gap between R1 and R3 is the time to go once around the Earth, about 40,000 km: it is the same at every station and measures the circumference directly.
laps.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: no long-way and repeat arrivals, or an R1-to-R3 gap that changes from one station to another.
radius.title: The Earth's radius, from 479 real seismic arrivals
radius.mini: 479 real surface-wave arrivals from nine earthquakes, one wave speed, nothing fitted: the median radius comes out at 6,910 km, 8.5% from the true 6,371 km. A flat Earth has an infinite radius.
radius.text: 479 real Rayleigh-wave arrivals, picked by seismograph networks for nine earthquakes between 2004 and 2022 and published in the International Seismological Centre's bulletin [1]. Only arrivals in the standard 18–22 s band are kept [2]. Each arrival gives a distance in degrees and a travel time; with one round wave speed of 3.5 km/s [3], each gives an Earth radius. One box per earthquake, then all 479 together, with the true 6,371 km drawn as a line. The medians run from 6,095 to 7,817 km, and the pooled median is 6,910 km, 8.5% high. The spread is real: this wave runs faster under oceans than under continents, and one speed for every path ignores that. Nothing was fitted.
radius.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: radii that grow without limit, since a plane is a sphere of infinite radius. The nine earthquakes' medians stay between 6,095 and 7,817 km.
radius-corr.title: The Earth's radius, corrected for oceans and continents
radius-corr.mini: Same 479 real arrivals, but each path gets its own speed from how much ocean it crosses. The median radius tightens from 6,910 to 6,675 km, 4.8% from the true 6,371 km.
radius-corr.text: The same 479 real arrivals from nine earthquakes [1]. A 20-second surface wave runs faster under thin oceanic crust than under thick continental crust. For each path, the fraction that crosses open ocean is measured on real coastlines [3], and two published speeds are mixed accordingly: 3.6 km/s for oceans and 2.97 km/s for continents [2]. Neither number was fitted to these data. The pooled median radius moves from 6,910 km to 6,675 km, 4.8% from the true 6,371 km, and every earthquake's box moves toward the line. The correction is coarse (real crust also varies with age, thickness and temperature), so the fit is closer, not perfect.
radius-corr.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: a correction for a real, independent cause that pushed the radius away from 6,371 km, or toward infinity.
radius-both.title: Measuring the Earth with earthquakes
radius-both.labels: One speed for every path|Speed set by the ocean share of each path
radius-both.mini: 479 real seismic arrivals, nine earthquakes. One wave speed gives a median Earth radius of 6,910 km. A speed per path, set by how much ocean it crosses, gives 6,675 km. The true value is 6,371 km.
radius-both.text: 479 real Rayleigh-wave arrivals from nine earthquakes between 2004 and 2022, from the International Seismological Centre's bulletin [1]. Each arrival gives a distance and a time, so with a wave speed, an Earth radius. With one speed for every path, a round 3.5 km/s [2]: the pooled median is 6,910 km, 8.5% high. With each path's speed set by the share of it that crosses ocean, measured on real coastlines [4], and two published speeds, 3.6 km/s for oceans and 2.97 km/s for continents [3], the median tightens to 6,675 km, 4.8% high. Nothing was fitted to these data. A flat Earth would need an infinite radius.
radius-both.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: radii that grow without limit. Both methods land within a few percent of 6,371 km.
reg.title: One earthquake, every arrival plotted twice
reg.mini: Each real arrival plotted at its recorded time, twice: at its distance on the globe and at its distance on the flat map. The globe's points line up at the wave's speed; the flat map's scatter.
reg.text: One real earthquake from the International Seismological Centre's bulletin [1], named above. Each real arrival is plotted at its recorded time, twice: at its great-circle distance (dark dot) and at the distance the flat-earth map gives between the same two coordinates (orange dot), joined by a thin line. The black line is a least-squares fit through the great-circle points alone, assuming no wave speed; its slope is the fitted speed, to compare with the reference line at 3.5 km/s. The flat map's points have no line of their own: each sits wherever that map's distortion puts it. With few stations the fit is noisy; pooled over all nine earthquakes it lands close to the speed line.
reg.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: the orange points lining up on a single speed line while the great-circle points scatter.
late.title: The flat map's error has a shape
late.mini: 479 real arrivals, sorted by the station's distance from the North Pole. The globe predicts every arrival to within 6.4 minutes on average. The flat map falls further behind toward the south, up to 68 minutes late.
late.text: For each of 479 real arrivals from nine earthquakes [1], two predictions are compared with the same recorded time: the globe's (great-circle distance at 3.5 km/s) and the flat map's (its own distance, same speed). The averages are plotted against the station's colatitude: 0° at the North Pole, 180° at the South Pole, which is where each station sits on the flat map. The globe stays within 6.4 minutes of the real clocks everywhere, with no trend; it is not exactly zero, because one round speed ignores the wave's real variation. The flat map is right near the pole and grows later toward the south, reaching 68 minutes near the far rim. That is the distortion of the map's own projection.
late.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: a flat-map error that stays flat across colatitude while the globe's error grows.
flatmaps.title: Give the flat Earth any map it likes: one map, nine earthquakes
flatmaps.labels: One earthquake on the chosen map|Every possible map centre
flatmaps.mini: Nine earthquakes relocated from their P-wave arrival times alone. On the globe they scatter by 1.8 s. On the best flat map, chosen out of the whole Earth, 7.3 s; on the North Pole map, 12 s.
flatmaps.text: From the International Seismological Centre's bulletins [1], only the time each P wave reached each station and the stations' latitudes and longitudes are kept. Each model gets the same freedom: a centre for each earthquake and a free curve of time against distance, along the great circle on the globe and straight across the disc on the flat map. An azimuthal equidistant map [2] keeps distances from its centre exact, so on a map centred on an earthquake that earthquake fits as well as on the globe. But a flat Earth has one map. Refitting all nine on every possible map centre, the best one, near 58° N 141° E, still scatters four times more than the globe, and the North Pole map almost seven times. To get even there, the flat curve must fall with distance for several earthquakes: the wave would reach farther stations sooner. Continents from Natural Earth [3].
flatmaps.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: one flat map fitting all nine earthquakes as well as the globe, with the same number of free parameters.
shadow.title: The ring of silence: where the core hides the P wave, station by station
shadow.labels: How the waves travel|The globe|The chosen flat map
shadow.mini: 12,822 stations of nine earthquakes. On the globe, direct P waves stop 103° from the epicentre, with nothing fitted: one ring at 97° for all nine leaves 53 stations on the wrong side. The best flat map, one ring for all nine, leaves 606.
shadow.text: A P wave dives through the mantle and comes back up out to about 103° from the epicentre. Beyond, the core is in the way: only a weak wave bent along it (Pdif) and, past about 143°, waves refracted through the liquid core (PKP) arrive. Each station of the International Seismological Centre's bulletins [1] is put in one group by the phases it reported. On the globe the shadow is a ring at a fixed angle around every epicentre [2][3]; the 103° edge is the textbook's, not fitted. On a flat map [5] the shadow is a disc around the epicentre whose radius is fitted, and the map centre is free. A map centred on one earthquake fits that earthquake exactly, but fails the others. The best single map, with one ring for the nine, misplaces eleven times as many stations as the globe's single angle. The phase names come from the ak135 tables, built for a spherical Earth [4], and the coordinates from maps: a check, not a measurement. Continents from Natural Earth [6].
shadow.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: one flat map on which one ring around each epicentre sorts the stations with and without a direct P as well as the globe's single angle does.
mesh.title: Does a shape come out of earthquake times alone?
mesh.mini: 138 stations placed from 19,813 P readings, no coordinate and no radius: a plane settles at 13.9 s, space at 1.4 s, on a sphere. Changing the speed only changes the size.
mesh.text: Every P arrival of 261 great earthquakes at the 138 stations that read at least 120 of them is a time and nothing else [1]. Every earthquake and station is a free point, on a plane or in space, moved until the times fit one law (a free origin time per earthquake, one free curve for all) [2]. The plane stays at 13.9 s rms of the time residuals; space settles at 1.4 s, with the stations within 0.4 % of a sphere's radius and, laid on the real map after the fact, 0.7° from their published positions, which the fit never read. Then the speed is changed on the settled cloud: a uniform change only scales it (R = 580 × v₀ km; the Earth's 6,371 km needs 11.0 km/s, a speed established with globe distances), while other laws leave a sphere but move its radius from 3.7 to 8.7 units and worsen the fit. The animation forces the plane first, then frees the third dimension from the same start; the arcs are drawn only once the sphere is there. Once the cloud is turned onto the real map (rotation only), each station's error is drawn in red. The times give the sphere; the speed gives its size. With every station that read at least 5 of the quakes, 6,951 stations and 186,610 readings kept, the shape does not change: space settles at 1.05 s, the plane at 11.8 s.
mesh.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: a plane that fits these times as well as space does, or a cloud in space that is not a sphere.
